newsitem.title: SWEDEN: U.S. may withdraw one carrier from Gulf, Perry says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may withdraw one carrier from Gulf, Perry says.

text.p: The United States may decide next week to remove one of its two aircraft carriers from the Gulf because Iraq appears to be backing away from a confrontation with Washington, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Sunday.

"All of the evidence that I have seen in the last four or five days is positive," he said, adding that a decision would be made next week on whether to return the carrier Carl Vinson to the United States on normal rotation in October, leaving only the carrier Enterprise in the strategic waterway.
U.S. officials who asked not to be identified said they expected the decision to be made during the first week of October.

"I truly believe that Iraq is backing off of the threatening actions they were taking a week ago. But we will watch it very carefully, very carefully, every day, every hour," Perry told reporters travelling with him aboard his aircraft from Helsinki to Stockholm.

The Enterprise was moved into the Gulf last week from the Mediterranean to join the Carl Vinson as part of a rapid build- up of U.S. forces in a confrontation between Baghdad and Washington after Iraqi forces attacked Kurds in the northern part of the country.

"We have no plans at this time to send any more forces than we have already sent in (to the Gulf) and we will make a decision about the carrier next week based on what happens between now and next week," Perry said.
In Kuwait, meanwhile, U.S. army captain Tim Raymond told Reuters the United States will complete its deployment of some 3,000 soldiers to the Gulf oil state by Monday.
About 400 of the soldiuers arrived in Kuwait on Sunday, raising the total number of U.S. troops already there to 2,500.
The Vinson had been scheduled to return to its home base at Bremerton, Washington, in October following six months at sea, U.S. officials said.

Iraq promised recently as tensions rose that it would no longer fire anti-aircraft missiles at U.S. and allied warplanes patrolling no-fly zones in Iraq, and those incidents have stopped in the past week.

The United States also deployed more than 3,000 troops and eight radar-avoiding F-117A stealth fighters to Iraq and moved big B-52 bombers to the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia as well as F-16 fighters to Bahrain in the confrontation.

"I have been in continual touch with our operations centre" in the Pentagon, Perry told reporters on the second leg of a 10-day trip that will carry him later to Denmark and to Norway for a NATO defence milisters meeting.
"Things remain quiet in Iraq. We continue to conduct the Operation Southern Watch flights over southern Iraq -- have had no problems with that," he added.

The White House, State Department and Pentagon have all said in recent statements that the situation in Iraq, which earlier this month prompted U.S. cruise missile attacks against air defences in southern Iraq, appeared to be calming down.

The United States has sent two written warnings to Iraqi President Saddam Hussein warning him to not to rebuild air defences destroyed by cruise missiles in the south, and CIA Director John Deutch told Congress last week that Iraq was moving its anti-aircraft units back to garrison.

But Deutch also told Congress, despite claims by the Clinton administration that its Iraqi military policy was successful, that the Iraqi leader -- whose forces were badly beaten by a U.S.-led military coalition in the 1991 Gulf War -- was now stronger politically based on his recent incursion into the north.
